title: Majestic Zugzwang
reviewNotes: Late twenty source diagrams and native complete ...Rxh5 position at 51 seconds reviewed. All eight pieces preserved. A finite legal strategy proves h4 against every one of eight Black replies: six sideways rook moves allow winning captures, ...Rxh4 gives an exact seven-piece White win, and ...Ke8 allows actual eight-piece Rc8 mate. Three source/independent branches show king retreat, ...Re5+ and ...Rb5. This composition repeats the other two batch sources. Earlier nine-piece setup remains outside proof.
transcript: The genius of white comes up with rook to c7, and the king cannot take this rook because otherwise he would lose his rook, and now the bishop will win the game. Instead, black comes up with an ingenious plan, rook to g8. And now if white is careless and simply moves the rook anywhere, this fork [music] is going to pick up the bishop. And after the king moves, this is simply a draw. And unfortunately, if we move anything else, [music] now the king is going to be able to take the rook for free. So, has white made a mistake? Is this now a draw? Well, not exactly. White has fighting spirit, and he plays on with the rook to c4. A move that doesn't seem to make sense. Doesn't this still allow the fork of the king and bishop? Yes, it does. But white follows up with king to e6. Another seemingly mysterious move. The bishop simply falls. What is the plan of white here? Well, black missed an incredible resource in this [music] position. As white plays the brilliant and beautiful >> [music] >> h4, and suddenly a shiver goes down the spine of the player with the black pieces as he realizes that this rook cannot go anywhere on this line, and he cannot take this pawn, meaning that the only move available to black is king to e8. But of course, this will fail to this beautiful checkmate.
